claim: Mesotrode integrates chronic wide-field mesoscale cortical imaging and compact multi-site cortical/subcortical cellular electrophysiology in head-fixed mice.
source: Here, we present Mesotrode that integrates chronic wide-field mesoscale cortical imaging and compact multi-site cortical/subcortical cellular electrophysiology in head-fixed mice that undergo self-initiated running or orofacial movements.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the developed technique.

claim: Mesotrode can characterize chronic single-neuron-related functional connectivity maps for up to 60 days post-implantation.
source: Using this approach, we were able to characterize chronic single-neuron-related functional connectivity maps for up to 60 days post-implantation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the results.

claim: Neurons recorded from distinct subcortical structures display diverse but segregated cortical maps.
source: Neurons recorded from distinct subcortical structures display diverse but segregated cortical maps, suggesting that neurons of different origins participate in distinct cortico-subcortical pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by clustering analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Facial nerve spiking is functionally associated with the PTA, RSP, and M2 network.
source: We extended the capability of Mesotrode by implanting the micro-electrode at the facial motor nerve and found that facial nerve spiking is functionally associated with the PTA, RSP, and M2 network
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spike-triggered average maps in Figure 6.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of the PTA area significantly reduced the facial movement of mice.
source: optogenetic inhibition of the PTA area significantly reduced the facial movement of the mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 7.

claim: Large-scale cortical network activity is dynamically sculpted by local or long-range inputs from individual neurons in various cortical or subcortical structures.
source: In the mammalian brain, large-scale cortical network activity is dynamically sculpted by local or long-range inputs from individual neurons in various cortical or subcortical structures (Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koch et al., 2016.

claim: Activities of single neurons are functionally coupled to those of local microcircuits or the global cortical networks.
source: Emerging studies using in vivo electrophysiological and imaging techniques have revealed that activities of single neurons are functionally coupled to those of local microcircuits or the global cortical networks, and such connectivity is dynamically regulated depending on the behavioral state of the animal (Barson et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2013a; Xiao et al., 2017; Clancy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chronic extracellular recordings in rodent brains were achieved most widely using bundled microwires called tetrodes.
source: Previously, chronic extracellular recordings in rodent brains were achieved most widely using bundled microwires called tetrodes, and more recently extended to the use of high-throughput recording devices such as silicon probes including Neuropixels (Bragin et al., 2000; Nguyen et al., 2009; Vandecasteele et al., 2012; Voigts et al., 2013; Delcasso et al., 2018; Juavinett et al., 2019; Steinmetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing previous work.

claim: Conventional chronic tetrode recording setups include a microdrive that provides axial control over the positioning of the electrodes.
source: In the case of conventional chronic tetrode recording setups, a common feature is the inclusion of a microdrive that provides axial control over the positioning of the electrodes which allows the electrode position to be adjusted for better recording qualities throughout the experimental periods.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about conventional tetrode setups.

claim: The microdrive in conventional tetrode setups hinders simultaneous wide-field optical imaging of the cortex.
source: However, this microdrive hinders simultaneous wide-field optical imaging of the cortex, making it difficult to investigate the correlation between subcortical single-unit activation and cortical network activity.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of conventional approaches that motivates the development of Mesotrode.

claim: GCaMP6 is a genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator widely used to optically record suprathreshold neuronal activation due to its high sensitivity and optimal signal-to-noise ratio.
source: To obtain high-resolution wide-field imaging of mouse brain activity, we chose to utilize GCaMP6, a genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator (GECI) widely used to optically record suprathreshold neuronal activation due to its high sensitivity and optimal signal-to-noise ratio (Chen et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013b.

claim: GECIs can stably report neuronal activity over several months.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that GECIs can stably report neuronal activity over several months (Huber et al., 2012; Margolis et al., 2012; Silasi et al., 2016), making them ideal for chronic studies of cortical network dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neurons from various subcortical structures, including the hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and other midbrain areas, display distinct functional connectivity patterns with the cortex.
source: We found that neurons from various subcortical structures, including the hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and other midbrain areas, display distinct functional connectivity patterns with the cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The spike-triggered maps (STMs) of recorded neurons can be stable for up to two months.
source: More importantly, we show that the spike-triggered maps (STMs) of recorded neurons can be stable for up to two months.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Tetrodes were fabricated from tungsten wires which were then soldered to a miniature connector that was cemented onto the back of the mouse skull during surgery.
source: Briefly, we fabricated tetrodes from tungsten wires which were then soldered to a miniature connector that was cemented onto the back of the mouse skull during surgery (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the fabrication procedure used in the study.

claim: The single tetrode was stiff enough to be straightly inserted into the deep brain areas through a small burr hole (<1 mm).
source: The single tetrode was stiff enough to be straightly inserted into the deep brain areas through a small burr hole (<1 mm; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mice were group-housed after the surgery.
source: As the miniature connectors are low-profile, mice were group-housed after the surgery (Figure 1C), and we did not observe significant damage to the window or the connectors after long-term monitoring.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The tetrodes can be flexibly implanted in almost any brain structure of interest, either cortical or subcortical.
source: The tetrodes can be flexibly implanted in almost any brain structure of interest, either cortical or subcortical.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the technique.

claim: High-quality recordings were successfully obtained in the mouse cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and midbrain.
source: We have successfully obtained high-quality recordings in the mouse cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and midbrain.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the technique.

claim: The recording site of each tetrode is confirmed using post-hoc histological analysis.
source: The recording site of each tetrode is confirmed using post-hoc histological analysis (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The single unit activity was relatively stable during 1 week, 2 weeks, and 2 months of recordings after implantation.
source: We found that the single unit activity was relatively stable during 1 week, 2 weeks, and 2 months of recordings after implantation (Figure 1F and G), which is consistent with previously reported chronic tetrode recordings in mice (Tolias et al., 2007; Hong and Lieber, 2019; Kim et al., 2020; Voigts et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 1F and G, and supported by citations.

claim: A total of 29 tetrodes were implanted in the midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and cortex of 14 mice.
source: We implanted a total of 29 tetrodes in the midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and cortex of 14 mice, and recorded the activity of 110 neurons with simultaneous mesoscale cortical imaging for up to 2 months after implantation (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental sample size.

claim: 110 neurons were recorded with simultaneous mesoscale cortical imaging for up to 2 months after implantation.
source: We implanted a total of 29 tetrodes in the midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, striatum, and cortex of 14 mice, and recorded the activity of 110 neurons with simultaneous mesoscale cortical imaging for up to 2 months after implantation (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental sample size and duration.

claim: On average, 3–5 neurons per tetrode were obtained, and this yield was consistent across regions.
source: On average, we obtained 3–5 neurons per tetrode implanted, and this yield was consistent across regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inter-spike interval (ISI) of neurons recorded from most brain regions ranged between 0.2 and 0.7 s.
source: The inter-spike interval (ISI) of neurons recorded from most brain regions ranged between 0.2 and 0.7 s, except for neurons of the striatum, which fires significantly less compared to neurons in other brain regions (Figure 2D, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Neurons of the striatum fire significantly less compared to neurons in other brain regions.
source: The inter-spike interval (ISI) of neurons recorded from most brain regions ranged between 0.2 and 0.7 s, except for neurons of the striatum, which fires significantly less compared to neurons in other brain regions (Figure 2D, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of ISI was similar across brain regions.
source: The coefficient of variation (CV) of ISI, a metric that indicates the consistency of the firing rate, was similar across brain regions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Spike-triggered average mapping (STM) has been previously used to investigate functional connectivity between single spiking neurons and cortical networks.
source: Spike-triggered average mapping (STM) has been previously used to investigate functional connectivity between single spiking neurons and cortical networks (Barson et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2017; Clancy et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous STM studies have only been achieved using acute preparation.
source: However, this has only been achieved using acute preparation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.

claim: Green reflectance signals were used to correct hemodynamic artifacts.
source: Green reflectance signals, which were recorded with the same frequency as the GCaMP6 signal, were used to correct hemodynamic artifacts (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach shown in Figure 3.

claim: Single neuron defined functional maps were stable across recording sessions and days.
source: We found that single neuron defined functional maps were stable across recording sessions and days.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: The STM of a hippocampus neuron was associated with the RSP, BCS, and M2 region for 10 recording sessions on different days.
source: For example, the STM of a hippocampus neuron was associated with the RSP, BCS, and M2 region for 10 recording sessions on different days (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Mesonet is a machine-learning based toolbox for parcellating brain regions.
source: To better visualize the stability of STMs across recording, we used Mesonet, a machine-learning based toolbox for parcellating brain regions, to accurately align our mesoscale images to a common brain atlas (Xiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a tool used in the analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: The STMs of a midbrain neuron were relatively stable over 2 months.
source: We show that the STMs of a midbrain neuron were relatively stable over 2 months (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The spiking activity of a midbrain neuron on different days was highly correlated with the lower limb, upper limb, and trunk sensorimotor areas on both hemispheres of the cortex.
source: The spiking activity of the neuron on different days was highly correlated with the lower limb, upper limb, and trunk sensorimotor areas on both hemispheres of the cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate and patterns of a midbrain neuron were highly correlated with the paw movement of the mouse.
source: In this example, we show that the instantaneous firing rate and patterns of this midbrain neuron were highly correlated with the paw movement of the mouse, consistent with our finding that this neuron is functionally associated with the limb sensorimotor areas.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A total of 1146 STMs of 110 neurons recorded during multiple sessions were included in the clustering analysis.
source: In total, we included 1146 STMs of 110 neurons recorded during multiple sessions.
evidence: This describes the dataset used for clustering analysis.

claim: Phenograph clustering resulted in 10 clusters with each cluster representing a distinct STM pattern.
source: This resulted in 10 clusters with each cluster representing a distinct STM pattern evidenced by their within-cluster averaged map (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the result of the clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 94 out of 1146 STMs were excluded from the clustering analysis.
source: Un-matched STMs that were below the similarity threshold (Pearson's correlation <0.3) compared to any of the 10 cluster average maps were excluded (94 out of 1146 STMs).
evidence: This describes the data filtering process.

claim: Individual STMs within the clusters showed high similarity to the cluster average maps.
source: For all clusters, individual STMs within the clusters showed high similarity to the cluster average maps (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: K-means clustering with Silhouette score confirmed that 10 clusters are most appropriate.
source: In order to validate the optimal number of clusters for partitioning our dataset, we evaluated the clustering effectiveness of a varied number of clusters when applying K-means clustering algorithm using Silhouette score (Rousseeuw, 1987) and confirmed that 10 clusters are most appropriate (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes a validation analysis shown in Figure 5C, supported by a citation.

claim: STMs of cortical neurons were primarily assigned to clusters #1–3 and #5–7, corresponding to motor, barrel, and primary somatosensory cortex activation patterns.
source: For example, STMs of cortical neurons were primarily assigned to clusters #1–3 and #5–7, corresponding to motor, barrel, and primary somatosensory cortex activation patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: The functional connectivity patterns of cortical neurons were localized to cortical areas surrounding the recorded neuron.
source: These activation areas also matched the locations of the recorded cortical neurons (e.g. motor cortical neurons showed motor area activated STMs), suggesting that the functional connectivity patterns of cortical neurons were localized to cortical areas surrounding the recorded neuron, which is consistent with previous reports (Xiao et al., 2017; Clancy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: 59.6% of all hippocampal neuron STMs primarily displayed STMs with retrosplenial cortex activation (cluster#10).
source: Hippocampal neurons primarily displayed STMs with retrosplenial cortex activation (cluster#10, 59.6% of all hippocampal neuron STMs), reaffirming the dense functional connectivity between these two regions (Karimi Abadchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by a citation.

claim: 47.7% of striatal neuron STMs showed a global activation except for the body (limb and trunk) somatosensory regions (cluster#4).
source: STMs of striatal neurons were dominated by two opposing patterns, where 47.7% of them showed a global activation except for the body (limb and trunk) somatosensory regions (cluster#4) and 28.8% of them showed only activation in the body sensory regions (cluster#9).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: 28.8% of striatal neuron STMs showed only activation in the body sensory regions (cluster#9).
source: STMs of striatal neurons were dominated by two opposing patterns, where 47.7% of them showed a global activation except for the body (limb and trunk) somatosensory regions (cluster#4) and 28.8% of them showed only activation in the body sensory regions (cluster#9).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Thalamic neurons exhibited diverse STM patterns with the primary activated regions in lateral anterior cortical regions and medial cortical regions.
source: Thalamic neurons exhibited diverse STM patterns with the primary activated regions in lateral anterior cortical regions (cluster#5, 5.6%, cluster#6, 23.3%, cluster#7 26.3% of all thalamic STMs) and medial cortical regions (cluster#8, 6.5%, cluster#9, 11.6%, cluster#10, 9.9% of all thalamic STMs).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Thalamic neurons had diverse functional connectivity patterns in relation to the dorsal cortex, consistent with previous studies.
source: This suggested that thalamic neurons had diverse functional connectivity patterns in relation to the dorsal cortex, consistent with previous studies (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings and supported by a citation.

claim: 44.6% of midbrain neuron STMs were most assigned to cluster#8 with medial frontal and somatosensory cortex activation.
source: STMs of midbrain neurons were most assigned to cluster#8 with medial frontal and somatosensory cortex activation (cluster#8, 44.6% of all midbrain STMs), but also included functional connectivity patterns with various other cortical regions (cluster#6, 10.5%, cluster#9, 12.6%, cluster#10, 11.2% of all midbrain STMs).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Neurons of different subcortical origins sometimes have overlapping STMs (e.g. cluster#9, and #10 exhibited by neurons from all subcortical regions).
source: Interestingly, we found that neurons of different subcortical origins sometimes have overlapping STMs (e.g. cluster#9, and #10 exhibited by neurons from all subcortical regions), which suggests that they may be involved in the same subcortico-cortical functional pathway (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Micro-wires were implanted on the facial motor nerve to record the spiking activity of the axonal projections from the facial motor neurons.
source: Here, we implanted micro-wires on the facial motor nerve to record the spiking activity of the axonal projections from the facial motor neurons (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: A distinct cortical pattern, activation in RSP, M2, and PTA areas, was associated with facial motor nerve spiking activity in awake mice showing spontaneous movements.
source: Surprisingly, we found a distinct cortical pattern, activation in RSP, M2, and PTA areas (Table 1), associated with facial motor nerve spiking activity (Figure 6C, D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Video 3) in awake mice showing spontaneous movements.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 6C, D, E and supplementary figures.

claim: A broad area of the dorsal cortex, including the PTA region, could evoke facial motor nerve spiking activity when optogenetically stimulated.
source: Using automated light-based mapping technology (Ayling et al., 2009), we found a broad area of the dorsal cortex, including the PTA region could evoke facial motor nerve spiking activity when optogenetically stimulated (Figure 6F, G and H, Figure 6—figure supplements 2–7, Video 4) within Thy1-ChR2 mice (n=6 mice).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 6F, G, H and supplementary figures, supported by a citation.

claim: Inhibiting the PTA not only stopped the PTA neurons from firing but also prevented the facial movements of mice when the blue light stimulation was on.
source: Echoing our previous finding, inhibiting the PTA not only stopped the PTA neurons from firing but also prevented the facial movements of these mice when the blue light stimulation was on (Figure 7, Video 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 7 and Video 5.

claim: Neuron firing in M1 and the barrel cortex (BCS) was not decreased by PTA inhibition.
source: To eliminate the possibility that this observation is due to indirect inhibition of other brain areas, we simultaneously recorded neuronal activities in M1 and the barrel cortex (BCS). We confirmed that the neuron firing in these brain areas was not decreased by PTA inhibition (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated as a control experiment shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: A 'rebound effect', a sudden increase in PTA neuron firing and facial movement, occurred right after the stimulation is turned off.
source: More interestingly, we saw a 'rebound effect', a sudden increase in PTA neuron firing and facial movement, right after the stimulation is turned off (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The 'off response' supports the causal relationships between PTA and facial movement.
source: This 'off response' supports the causal relationships between PTA and facial movement.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the rebound effect.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous reports that the PTA is involved in controlling active movements.
source: These findings are consistent with the previous report that the PTA is involved in controlling active movements (Chapman et al., 2002; Cohen and Andersen, 2002; Rathelot et al., 2017; Auffret et al., 2018; Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019; Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activities of cortical pyramidal neurons are known to be coupled to local network activity.
source: Activities of cortical pyramidal neurons are known to be coupled to local network activity; as such, STMs of these neurons often display activity motifs localized to the cortical regions they reside, indicating that their functional connections are mostly involved in local networks (Xiao et al., 2017; Clancy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Subcortical neurons (i.e. thalamic neurons) can display more diverse and distal connectivity patterns with cortical networks that are less confined by their locations.
source: On the other hand, subcortical neurons (i.e. thalamic neurons) can display more diverse and distal connectivity patterns with cortical networks that are less confined by their locations (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: The connectivity patterns of neurons in different subcortical structures are varied.
source: Furthermore, by classifying these STMs, we found that the connectivity patterns of neurons in different subcortical structures are varied.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: STMs of midbrain neurons can be primarily categorized into 4 classes, with each class having distinct activity motifs.
source: For instance, STMs of midbrain neurons can be primarily categorized into 4 classes, with each class having distinct activity motifs, which is in contrast to the striatum neurons, the STMs of which are grouped into only two main classes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: STMs of striatum neurons are grouped into only two main classes.
source: For instance, STMs of midbrain neurons can be primarily categorized into 4 classes, with each class having distinct activity motifs, which is in contrast to the striatum neurons, the STMs of which are grouped into only two main classes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: STMs of different subcortical regions display low levels of overlap, suggesting that neurons of different subcortical origins form their own distinct connectivity pattern to the cortex.
source: More interestingly, STMs of different subcortical regions display low levels of overlap, suggesting that neurons of different subcortical origins form their own distinct connectivity pattern to the cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and interpretation from the clustering analysis.

claim: The single neuron defined functional maps (STMs) can reveal functional cortical architecture related to the activity of individual cortical and subcortical-cortical neurons.
source: The single neuron defined functional maps (STMs) can reveal functional cortical architecture related to the activity of individual cortical and subcortical-cortical neurons (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation and supported by a citation.

claim: The distinct STM patterns indicate that single neuron embedded large-scale subcortico-cortical networks may be associated with specific brain functions.
source: The distinct STM patterns indicate that single neuron embedded large-scale subcortico-cortical networks may be associated with specific brain functions (Pessoa, 2014; Liu et al., 2021a; Amunts et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation and supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies using anterograde virus tracing have revealed that the motor cortex sends few direct projections to the facial nucleus.
source: Previous studies using anterograde virus tracing have revealed that the motor cortex sends few direct projections to the facial nucleus while the most prominent projections from the motor, somatosensory, and association cortex are polysynaptic, presumably through nuclei in the brainstem (Grinevich et al., 2005; Matyas et al., 2010; Rathelot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The most prominent projections from the motor, somatosensory, and association cortex to the facial nucleus are polysynaptic, presumably through nuclei in the brainstem.
source: Previous studies using anterograde virus tracing have revealed that the motor cortex sends few direct projections to the facial nucleus while the most prominent projections from the motor, somatosensory, and association cortex are polysynaptic, presumably through nuclei in the brainstem (Grinevich et al., 2005; Matyas et al., 2010; Rathelot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Studies in humans and monkeys have identified parietal-eye-field and reach-specific areas that involve voluntary control of eye or hand movement.
source: Studies in humans and monkeys have identified parietal-eye-field and reach-specific areas that involve voluntary control of eye or hand movement (Lynch, 1980; Andersen, 1989; Sakata et al., 1997; Chapman et al., 2002; Konen and Kastner, 2008; Archambault et al., 2009; Pouget, 2015; Rathelot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The PTA region is involved in facial movements in mice.
source: Our findings suggest that the PTA region is also involved in facial movements in mice, and supplement the current understanding of the functional connectivity between cortex and facial nucleus motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Tetrodes were fabricated from polyimide insulated tungsten wire (40 cm long, diameter 25 μm).
source: Polyimide insulated, tungsten wire (40 cm long, diameter 25 μm, Stablohm 650, California Fine Wire, USA) was folded into four wires and clamped together with the modified alligator clip.
evidence: This describes the materials and methods used for tetrode fabrication.

claim: Eighty clockwise twists were applied and followed by forty counter clock-wise twists to the wire bundle during tetrode fabrication.
source: Eighty clockwise twists were applied and followed by forty counter clock-wise twists to the wire bundle over the course of approximately three minutes.
evidence: This describes the fabrication procedure.

claim: Transgenic GCaMP6s mice (n=19) were produced by crossing Emx1-cre, CaMK2-tTA and TITL-GCaMP6s strain.
source: Transgenic GCaMP6s mice (males, 2–4 months of age, weighing 20–30 g; n=19) were produced by crossing Emx1-cre (B6.129S2-Emx1tm1(cre)Krj/J, Jax #005628), CaMK2-tTA (B6.Cg-Tg(Camk2a-tTA)1Mmay/DboJ, Jax #007004) and TITL-GCaMP6s (Ai94;B6.Cg-Igs7tm94.1(tetO-GCaMP6s)Hze/J, Jax #024104) strain.
evidence: This describes the mouse strains used in the study.

claim: Channelrhodopsin-2 transgenic mice (n=6) were obtained from the Jackson Labs (line 18, stock 007612).
source: Channelrhodopsin-2 transgenic mice (Arenkiel et al., 2007) (n=6) were obtained from the Jackson Labs (line 18, stock 007612, strain B6.Cg-Tg(Thy1-COP4/EYFP)18Gfng/J).
evidence: This describes the mouse strains used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: VGAT-ChR2-YFP expressing mice (n=3) were used for optogenetic inhibition experiments.
source: Neuronal activity was driven by optically activating inhibitory neurons targeted in VGAT-ChR2-YFP expressing mice (Zhao et al., 2011; n=3).
evidence: This describes the mouse strains used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The tetrode signals were amplified using a 16-channel data acquisition system (20 kHz, USB-ME16-FAI-System, Multi-Channel Systems).
source: The tetrode signals were amplified using a 16-channel data acquisition system (20 kHz, USB-ME16-FAI-System, Multi-Channel Systems) and recorded for at least 30 min every day.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition system used.

claim: Data were high pass-filtered at 1 kHz for spike sorting.
source: Briefly, data were high pass-filtered at 1 kHz, and excitatory spikes were detected using a threshold of 4.5 times the median of the standard deviation over 0.675.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: Excitatory spikes were detected using a threshold of 4.5 times the median of the standard deviation over 0.675.
source: Briefly, data were high pass-filtered at 1 kHz, and excitatory spikes were detected using a threshold of 4.5 times the median of the standard deviation over 0.675.
evidence: This describes the spike detection procedure.

claim: The 12-bit images were captured at a frame rate of 120 Hz (exposure time of 7ms) with 8×8 on-chip spatial binning.
source: The 12-bit images were captured at a frame rate of 120 Hz (exposure time of 7ms) with 8×8 on-chip spatial binning using EPIX XCAP v3.8 imaging software.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used.

claim: Blue light (473 nm) with a bandpass filter (467–499 nm) was used to excite calcium indicators.
source: Blue light (473 nm) with a bandpass filter (467–499 nm) was used to excite calcium indicators and green light (525 nm) with a bandpass filter (525/50 nm) was used to observe changes in cerebral blood volume.
evidence: This describes the imaging methodology.

claim: Green light (525 nm) with a bandpass filter (525/50 nm) was used to observe changes in cerebral blood volume.
source: Blue light (473 nm) with a bandpass filter (467–499 nm) was used to excite calcium indicators and green light (525 nm) with a bandpass filter (525/50 nm) was used to observe changes in cerebral blood volume.
evidence: This describes the imaging methodology.

claim: The LED strobe frequency of 60 Hz exceeded the critical flicker fusion frequency for mice.
source: This LED strobe frequency of 60 Hz exceeded the critical flicker fusion frequency for mice, which marks the highest temporal frequency that an observer can resolve flicker before it becomes indistinguishable from constant light and was likely imperceptible to the mice.
evidence: This describes the imaging methodology and its rationale.

claim: 1 mW of optical stimulation was delivered for an overall time of 10 s for optogenetic inhibition experiments.
source: During the experiment, 1 mW (measured from the end of the cable) of optical stimulation was delivered for an overall time of 10 s.
evidence: This describes the optogenetic stimulation parameters.

claim: For automated Thy1-ChR2-based facial motor mapping, a flash of laser light (10ms, 2.0 mW) was delivered to each point in an 8x8 grid.
source: For automated Thy1-ChR2-based facial motor mapping, we chose a relatively collimated 473 nm laser targeted through a simple microscope. The laser was moved in random order to each of the predefined stimulation locations (8x8 grid) and delivered a flash of laser light (10ms, 2.0 mW) to each point while collecting facial motor nerve response.
evidence: This describes the optogenetic mapping procedure.

claim: PhenoGraph clustering only requires one input parameter which is k, the number of nearest neighbors to be found for each input vector.
source: This algorithm only requires one input parameter which is k, the number of nearest neighbors to be found for each input vector, and the resulting number of clusters (10) is relatively insensitive to the k chosen over the range of typically chosen values.
evidence: This describes the clustering algorithm used.

claim: An individual STM whose similarity (Pearson correlation value) with the cluster average STM of the assigned cluster was lower than 0.3 was manually reassigned or excluded.
source: We then performed a cluster identity refinement step, where an individual STM whose similarity (Pearson correlation value) with the cluster average STM of the assigned cluster was lower than 0.3 was manually reassigned if its similarity with group average STMs of any other clusters was higher than 0.3; otherwise, that STM was excluded.
evidence: This describes the data refinement procedure.

claim: Animal protocols (A13-0336-A22-0054 and A14-0266-A22-0258) were approved by the University of British Columbia Animal Care Committee.
source: Animal protocols (A13-0336-A22-0054 and A14-0266-A22-0258) were approved by the University of British Columbia Animal Care Committee and conformed to the Canadian Council on Animal Care and Use guidelines and animals were housed in a vivarium on a 12 h daylight cycle (7 AM lights on).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.
